titleStmt.title: Telegram From the Department of State to the Embassy in Ecuador

div.head: 368. Telegram From the Department of State to the Embassy in Ecuador
div.p: 30231. Subject: Conversation between Secretary Haig and Ecuadorean Foreign Minister Barrera.

2. Secretary Haig met for about 20 minutes at the OAS headquarters with Ecuadorean Foreign Minister Barrera on the morning of February 3. Accompanying Barrera was Ecuadoran Ambassador Crespo. Accompanying Haig were Bushnell and Eaton. The principal concentration of the conversation was on the Ecuador-Peru border conflict. Other subjects discussed were Central America and the US attitude toward the internal politics of other countries.

3. Barrera opened by expressing Ecuador’s sincere thanks for the US positive approach to the current dispute. Ecuador was in favor of a role for the US, Brazil, Argentina and Chile in the achievement and consolidation of peace but Ecuador was also convinced that there must be an Organization of American States involvement. Ecuador’s future attitude toward the OAS would be critically affected by whether or not it had a role. It wanted something in writing that would specify that the four countries presently involved in peacemaking were not acting solely (SIC) as guarantors but also as representatives of the OAS. It wanted to know the USG position on this point.

4. The Secretary noted that he had a special familiarity
with this issue because an Ecuadoran by the name of Roca from Guayaquil had been his roommate at West Point in 1944. He said it was most unfortunate that this conflict had developed now when the hemisphere was faced with other problems that were so serious. He welcomed the ceasefire and said that he hoped there could be a decoupling of forces because of the inadvertent return to hostilities that could occur if there were not a disengagement. He hoped the two parties could reach a solution to the problem between themselves. He recognized the overlapping of or contradictions between the two international forums in which the dispute was being discussed. He said that the US would have to look into the issue more closely.

5. Barrera said—in apparent reference to the aggressiveness and vehemence of his presentation before the OAS the night before—that he would be speaking in the OAS today in as constructive a tone as possible. He wanted to underscore that we are talking about an area where the US has no legally binding position because the Rio Protocol does not establish what the border is. Since there is no agreed border, peace in the area is precarious. The keeping of that peace should not be confined to the guarantors. He, therefore, asked the US support for three points: (1) that it is acting in this issue as a friendly country, (2) that the OAS has a role in addition to the four countries presently involved, and (3) that whatever commission is established be continued for years if necessary.

6. The Secretary replied that he would wish to consider the three points made by Ecuador with care before responding. He thought it important to move carefully and not too rapidly in such matters. He lauded Barrera for his reputation as a diplomat and said that it had been confirmed by his presentation.

7. Central America. The Secretary said that in only two weeks the Reagan Administration had verified a massive Cuban intervention in El Salvador principally through Nicaragua. This kind of intervention is unacceptable to this administration. It will adopt fundamentally different policies with regard to it. In this respect it will want to have unusually close and cordial consultations with other countries of the hemisphere and especially with friends like Ecuador. Barrera replied with apparent conviction
that he was in one hundred percent agreement. It was a fundamental principle of the hemisphere that there should be no intervention. Too often this was taken in Latin America to refer only to the US. Ecuador was convinced that it should apply to all countries. Ecuador does not see why any Latin American country should be exempt from this principle.

8. US attitude toward the internal politics of other countries. Secretary Haig said that the US had no preconceived ideas about the appropriate internal regimes of other countries and President Reagan would not try to impose the US model on other countries. Human rights are important but it is also important to concentrate on legal social change without foreign intervention.

note.p: Source: Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D810055–0755. Secret; Immediate; Exdis. Sent for information Immediate to Lima. Drafted by Eaton; cleared by Bushnell and in S/S, S/S–O; approved by Baltimore.

In telegram 19262 to Lima and Quito, January 24, the Department reported that Crespo had informed Eaton on January 23 that a “Peruvian helicopter had crossed border and shot at Ecuadorean helicopter on the ground, seriously wounding Ecuadorean pilot.” On January 24, Crespo telephoned Eaton and told him that “the situation looked bad,” as “Peru had mobilized on border and was threatening attack.” (Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D810036–0828) On February 10, Edward Schumacher wrote in the New York Times: “Ecuadorean soldiers were expelled from three border posts after five days of fighting in which Peru says one of its soldiers was killed and Ecuador says it lost eight, though the reliability of the figures and the reported ferocity of the fighting have been questioned. The outposts are up to nine miles past a line that the Peruvian and Ecuadorean armed forces informally drew as a cease-fire line after similar clashes three years ago. Sometime since then the Ecuadoreans secretly moved in and occupied the jungle posts. It was that occupation, discovered by Peruvian patrols more than two weeks ago, that led to the idea that Ecuador precipitated the incident.” (Edward Schumacher, “Behind Ecuador War, Long-Smoldering Resentment,” New York Times, February 10, 1981, p. A2) This five-day border war, known as the Paquisha War (or Fake Paquisha War), was a part of a centuries-old border dispute between Ecuador and Peru; see footnote 3, below.

In 1941 Peru successfully invaded Ecuador. The United States, Brazil, Argentina, and Chile helped to negotiate a peace treaty. The 1942 Rio de Janeiro Protocol, with the United States, Brazil, Argentina, and Chile serving as guarantor nations, ceded Ecuadorean territory to Peru and determined the border in the Cordillera del Cóndor. For the protocol between Ecuador and Peru regarding peace, friendship, and boundaries signed at Rio de Janeiro on January 29, 1942, see Department of State Executive Agreement Series No. 288, or 56 Stat. (pt. 2) 1818. During the Paquisha War (or Fake Paquisha War) the four countries helped to negotiate a cease-fire. See “Peru Claims Victory; Ecuador Says Battle Goes On,” New York Times, February 2, 1981, p. A1; and “Peru and Ecuador Agree to Cease-Fire,” Washington Post, February 3, 1981, p. A27. See also Document 414 and footnotes 3 and 4 thereto.

In a March 6 memorandum to Allen, Fontaine noted: “For the moment, this issue has been put on the back burner, but we are not very close to a settlement—even a temporary one.” Fontaine added: “The U.S. is considering sales of the F–5 or approval of the Israeli Kfir to Ecuador. Other things being equal either would be o.k. But this is not a case of ceritus paribus. The sale of U.S. F–5s in particular at this time would be very provocative, causing endless political grief for Belaunde Terry, the pro-American President of Peru. This matter must be very carefully reviewed—with the most important consideration which is political—dealt with as the highest priority.” (Reagan Library, Roger W. Fontaine Files, Chronological File, [03/05/1981–03/06/1981])
